title: The capital stack: equity, debt, mezzanine, who is paid first
summary: A project's money comes in layers, from the safest senior debt to the riskiest common equity, and each layer is paid in a fixed order. The order of payment decides who is protected when things go wrong and who earns the most when they go right.
body:
Bottom line. Every project is funded by a stack of money, and the stack is paid from the top down. Mr Shabazz, the lender at the top is paid first and earns the least; the equity at the bottom is paid last and earns the most, so your job is to know exactly where your own money sits and what has to go right before it comes back.

In plain English

The capital stack is the list of every source of money in a project, arranged in the order they are repaid. Think of it as a building turned upside down: the top floor is paid first.

Senior debt is the main loan, usually from a bank, secured by a first mortgage on the land. Security means a legal right to take and sell an asset if the loan is not paid. Mezzanine debt sits below the senior loan. It is often secured by a pledge of the shares of the company that owns the project, rather than by the land. Preferred equity is an ownership interest with a fixed priority return before common owners. Common equity is the owners' money, paid last and keeping whatever is left.

The rule that sets the order of payment is called the waterfall. Money flows to the top layer until it is full, then spills to the next.

The framework

For each layer, ask six questions.

  1. Priority. Who is paid before this layer, and who after?
  2. Return. What does it earn: fixed interest, a preferred return, or a share of profit?
  3. Security. What can it take if not paid: the land, the shares, or nothing?
  4. Control. What rights does it have: approval of budgets, the right to step in, or the right to replace the developer?
  5. Term. When must it be repaid or refinanced?
  6. Recourse. Can it reach beyond the project, for example through a personal guarantee? A personal guarantee is your promise to pay the debt yourself if the company does not.

Then read the document that ties the layers together. An intercreditor agreement sets the rules between the senior lender and the mezzanine lender: who can enforce, when, and what the junior lender may do to protect itself. Senior lenders often limit or forbid other debt unless such an agreement is signed.

Two principles follow. First, risk and return move together: the lower a layer sits, the higher the return it demands. Second, losses hit the bottom first: equity absorbs the first loss, then mezzanine, then senior debt.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A project costs a hypothetical $10,000,000. The stack is: senior debt $6,000,000, mezzanine debt $1,500,000, and common equity $2,500,000. For simplicity, ignore interest and fees.

Good case: the finished project sells for $13,000,000. Senior gets $6,000,000. Mezzanine gets $1,500,000. Equity gets the remaining $5,500,000, more than double its $2,500,000.

Weak case: the project sells for $9,000,000. Senior gets $6,000,000. Mezzanine gets $1,500,000. Equity gets $1,500,000 and has lost $1,000,000, or 40 percent.

Bad case: the project sells for $7,000,000. Senior gets $6,000,000. Mezzanine gets $1,000,000 and loses $500,000. Equity gets nothing. And if the developer signed a personal guarantee of the mezzanine loan, he may owe the $500,000 shortfall personally.

Notice that a 30 percent swing in sale price moved the equity from a large gain to a total loss. That leverage is the nature of the bottom of the stack.

Interest makes the picture harsher, not softer. Senior and mezzanine interest keeps adding up during a slow sale, and it is paid before equity. A project that takes a year longer than planned can move the equity from the weak case to the bad case without any change in the sale price at all.

Professional Sign-Off Required: lawyer (financing) and chartered professional accountant

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is looking only at the interest rate on each loan, rather than at the order of payment, the security and the control rights. A cheap mezzanine loan that can take your shares and replace you as developer after one missed payment may cost more than an expensive one without that right. The second mistake is signing personal guarantees casually, which turns a project loss into a personal one.

A third mistake is forgetting that preferred equity, despite its name, is still equity. It usually has no security over the land and cannot force a sale on its own, so its protection comes only from the contract. Read what it can actually do before you treat it as safe.

How you will use it

As a developer, draw the stack for every project before you sign any term sheet: each layer, its amount, its priority, its return, its security, its control rights and any guarantee. Then run three sale prices through the waterfall, as in the example, so you can see what each party receives. Show the drawing to your lawyer and ask which clauses in each document change the order or give a layer extra control. Negotiate guarantees last and narrowly: limit them in amount, in time, or to specific events such as fraud. Knowing the stack is how you know what you are really risking.
checklist: Draw every layer of the stack with its amount and priority
Record each layer's return, security and control rights
Identify every personal guarantee and its limits
Read the intercreditor agreement before adding junior debt
Run a good, weak and bad sale price through the waterfall
Check when each layer must be repaid or refinanced
Ask counsel which clauses change the order of payment

selftest.q: A hypothetical $5,000,000 project is funded with $3,000,000 senior debt, $1,000,000 mezzanine and $1,000,000 equity. It sells for $3,500,000. Who receives what, ignoring interest?
selftest.a: Senior debt is paid first and receives $3,000,000 in full. Mezzanine receives the remaining $500,000 and loses $500,000. Equity receives nothing and loses its full $1,000,000. Any personal guarantee of the mezzanine loan could make the developer personally liable for the $500,000 shortfall.

apply: Draw the capital stack for one project you have or plan, and write the order in which each layer would be paid.
sources: The capital stack, waterfall and intercreditor concepts are standard real estate finance practice and are not drawn from any statute. Actual rights depend on the loan, security and intercreditor documents. All figures are hypothetical. Education only, not financial or legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: lawyer (financing) and chartered professional accountant

title: Reading a lender: DSCR, LTV, covenants, bankability
summary: Lenders decide with a few ratios and a list of promises they make the borrower keep. If you calculate those ratios the way the lender does, before you ask, you can see whether a project is bankable and on what terms.
body:
Bottom line. A lender asks two questions: will the property's income pay the loan, and is the property worth more than the loan? Mr Shabazz, those questions become ratios called DSCR and LTV, and the answers become covenants you must keep for the life of the loan, so learn to compute them the lender's way before you walk in.

In plain English

Net operating income, or NOI, is the property's income after operating costs but before loan payments and income tax. Debt service is the total of principal and interest payments on the loan for a year.

The debt service coverage ratio, or DSCR, is NOI divided by debt service. A DSCR of 1.25 means the income covers the loan payments one and a quarter times. The loan-to-value ratio, or LTV, is the loan divided by the property's appraised value. The loan-to-cost ratio, or LTC, is the loan divided by the total project cost, which matters most during construction.

A covenant is a promise in the loan agreement. Breaking one is usually an event of default, which can let the lender demand repayment. Bankable means a project fits a lender's standard rules well enough to be financed on normal terms.

The framework

Read a lender in five steps.

  1. Underwriting NOI. The lender calculates NOI its own way. It often uses lower rents than your forecast, adds a vacancy allowance, adds a management fee even if you manage yourself, and adds a reserve for future repairs. Your NOI and the lender's NOI will differ, and only theirs counts.
  2. Coverage. The lender sets a minimum DSCR. It also often tests DSCR at an interest rate higher than the actual rate, which is called a stress rate.
  3. Leverage. The lender sets a maximum LTV on an appraisal it orders, and during construction a maximum LTC. The loan is the lowest amount that passes every test.
  4. Covenants. There are three kinds. Financial covenants require ratios to stay above or below set levels. Reporting covenants require statements, rent rolls and certificates by set dates. Negative covenants forbid things without consent, such as more debt, a sale, a change of control, or dividends while a test fails.
  5. Recourse and guarantees. Whether the lender can reach you or your other companies beyond the property.

Lenders also look at you: your track record, your equity in the deal, your liquidity, and how complete and organized your package is. Bankability is part numbers and part trust.

One more distinction matters. A construction loan is usually sized on cost and repaid from a sale or a permanent loan. A permanent loan, sometimes called a term loan, is sized on income once the building is leased. The permanent lender's DSCR test is what decides whether the construction loan can be repaid, so read both lenders' rules from the start.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A finished rental building has a forecast NOI of a hypothetical $700,000. The lender underwrites it at $600,000 after lower rents, vacancy, management and reserves.

The lender requires a minimum DSCR of 1.25 and a maximum LTV of 70 percent, and its appraisal values the building at $8,000,000.

The LTV test allows a loan of 70 percent of $8,000,000, which is $5,600,000. The DSCR test allows annual debt service of $600,000 divided by 1.25, which is $480,000. Suppose, at the lender's stress rate and amortization, $480,000 a year supports a loan of about $5,000,000. The loan offered is the lower of the two, $5,000,000.

If the developer budgeted on $5,600,000, he has a $600,000 equity gap. He learned it at the term sheet, not at closing, because he ran the lender's numbers first.

Professional Sign-Off Required: lawyer (financing) and mortgage broker or financing advisor

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is calculating DSCR on your own optimistic NOI and the actual interest rate, then being surprised when the lender offers less. The second mistake is reading only the rate and the amount in a term sheet and ignoring the covenants. A covenant that tests DSCR every quarter can put you in default in one weak quarter, even while every payment is made on time.

A third mistake is assuming the appraisal will match your own view of value. The lender orders its own appraisal, often on more cautious assumptions, and the loan follows that number.

How you will use it

As a developer, build a lender's version of every pro forma: lender-style NOI, the stress rate, the coverage test, the leverage test, and the lower of the resulting loan amounts. Use it to size your equity before you approach anyone. When a term sheet arrives, list every covenant with its test level, frequency and cure period, meaning the time allowed to fix a breach. Ask your lawyer to negotiate cure rights and sensible test dates. Then keep a covenant calendar after closing, with each report and certificate due, and check the ratios yourself before the lender does. A borrower who reports early and accurately is the borrower a lender wants to finance again.
checklist: Recalculate NOI the way a lender would, with vacancy, management and reserves
Test DSCR at a stressed interest rate, not only the actual rate
Calculate the loan allowed by each test and take the lowest
List every covenant with its test level, frequency and cure period
Check negative covenants on extra debt, sale, control and dividends
Identify any recourse or personal guarantee
Keep a covenant calendar after closing and test ratios before reporting

selftest.q: A lender underwrites NOI at a hypothetical $400,000, requires DSCR of 1.25 and allows 75 percent LTV on a $5,000,000 appraisal. Which test is likely to limit the loan, and how do you check?
selftest.a: The LTV test allows $3,750,000. The DSCR test allows debt service of $400,000 divided by 1.25, which is $320,000 a year. Convert $320,000 of annual payments into a loan amount using the lender's stress rate and amortization. Whichever loan amount is lower is the limit. Compare both before assuming either.

apply: Take one project and recompute its NOI the lender's way, then divide by 1.25 to see the most annual debt service that NOI supports.
sources: DSCR, LTV, LTC and covenant concepts are standard commercial lending practice, not statutory rules. Each lender sets its own tests, stress rates and definitions in its term sheet and loan agreement. All figures are hypothetical. Education only, not financial or legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: lawyer (financing) and mortgage broker or financing advisor

title: Pro forma discipline: sources and uses, sensitivities, the killing number
summary: A pro forma is a forecast, and its value lies in how honestly it is built and how hard it is tested. Sources must equal uses, every key input should be stressed, and you should know the one number that would kill the project.
body:
Bottom line. A pro forma is a forecast, not a fact. Mr Shabazz, its job is not to prove a project works; its job is to show where it breaks, so build it so sources equal uses, stress every key input, and find the killing number before anyone else does.

In plain English

A pro forma is a financial model that forecasts a project's costs, financing, income and returns. Sources and uses is a two-column table. Uses list every dollar the project will spend. Sources list every dollar that will pay for it. The two columns must be equal. If they are not, there is a gap that someone must fill.

A sensitivity is a test that changes one input, such as construction cost, and shows how the result changes. A scenario changes several inputs at once to reflect a plausible story, such as a recession. The killing number is the value of one input at which the project fails a test that matters, for example the rent at which the loan's coverage covenant would be breached.

The framework

  1. Uses, complete. Land, hard costs, soft costs such as design, permits, legal and financing fees, interest during construction, marketing, and a contingency. A contingency is money set aside for costs nobody can yet name.
  2. Sources, committed. Mark each source as committed, likely, or hoped for. Only committed sources count toward closing.
  3. Inputs, documented. Every key input should have a source: a contractor's estimate, an appraisal, market rent evidence, a lender's term sheet. Write the source and date beside each number.
  4. Sensitivities. Test at least construction cost, rent or sale price, interest rate, time to complete, and time to lease or sell.
  5. Killing numbers. For each key input, find the value at which equity is lost, a covenant is breached, or the sources no longer cover the uses.
  6. Distance to failure. Compare each killing number with the base case. A killing number that is close to the base case is the project's real risk.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A rental project has uses of a hypothetical $12,000,000, including a $600,000 contingency. Sources are $8,400,000 of senior debt, committed by term sheet, and $3,600,000 of equity, of which $2,400,000 is committed and $1,200,000 is hoped for.

First finding: the committed sources are $10,800,000 against $12,000,000 of uses. The project is not ready to close; a $1,200,000 gap remains.

Sensitivities: construction cost up 10 percent adds $1,000,000 of hard cost and uses most of the contingency plus $400,000 more. A one-point rise in the interest rate adds interest during construction and lowers the loan the lender will size on completion. A six-month delay adds interest and pushes back rent.

Killing numbers: the base case rent is a hypothetical $2.50 per square foot per month. At $2.20, the DSCR falls below the lender's covenant at completion and the permanent loan shrinks. That is only 12 percent below the base case. Construction cost can rise 15 percent before equity is wiped out on a sale.

The conclusion is clear: rent is the real risk. The developer seeks pre-leasing evidence and a fixed-price construction contract before committing more money.

Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant and, for value inputs, an accredited appraiser

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is building the pro forma backward, starting from the return you want and adjusting inputs until it appears. A model built that way proves nothing. The second mistake is leaving out costs that feel small, such as financing fees, interest during construction, and the developer's own time, which together can erase the margin.

A third mistake is testing one input at a time and stopping there. In real downturns, costs, rates and rents often move against you together. Run at least one combined scenario, such as costs up, rent down and a six-month delay at once, and see whether the project survives it. If it does not, decide in advance what you would do, such as reducing scope, bringing in a partner or pausing, so the decision is not made in a panic.

How you will use it

As a developer, keep one master pro forma per project with a sources and uses tab, an inputs tab showing the evidence and date for each number, and a sensitivity tab. Update it at every gate. Before any meeting with a lender or investor, run the killing numbers and write them at the top of the summary page. Investors trust a developer who shows them where a project breaks, because it proves the developer has looked. Use the killing numbers to decide what to fix first: if rent is closest to failure, buy rent certainty; if cost is closest, buy cost certainty. That is how a model becomes a decision tool rather than a sales document.

Finally, keep every version. When a lender or investor asks why a number changed, a dated history of the model shows that each change came from new evidence, not from a wish to make the result look better.
checklist: Make sources equal uses, to the dollar
Mark each source as committed, likely or hoped for
Write the evidence and date beside every key input
Include financing fees, interest during construction and a contingency
Run sensitivities on cost, rent or price, rate, delay and lease-up
Find the killing number for each key input
Put the killing numbers on the summary page

selftest.q: Your pro forma shows a strong return, but sources include $1,000,000 of equity that no investor has committed, and rent only needs to fall 8 percent to breach the lender's coverage covenant. What do these two facts tell you?
selftest.a: The project is not ready to close, because sources do not cover uses with committed money. And the real risk is rent, because the killing number is very close to the base case. The next steps are to secure committed equity and to buy rent certainty, such as pre-leasing, before spending more.

apply: Take one project model and find one killing number: the rent, price or cost at which the project fails, and how far it is from your base case.
sources: Sources and uses, sensitivity analysis and break-even testing are standard project finance and accounting practice, not statutory rules. All figures are hypothetical. Education only, not financial advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant and, for value inputs, an accredited appraiser

title: Gates and sequencing: what must be true before you ask for money
summary: Money should be raised in stages, each unlocked only when specific facts are proven, so that risk falls before larger amounts are committed. Asking for money before the gate is passed costs credibility, worse terms and sometimes legal trouble.
body:
Bottom line. A project should pass through gates, and each gate has a list of things that must be true before more money is asked for or spent. Mr Shabazz, raising money before the facts are proven gets worse terms, uses up credibility, and when the money comes from investors can create securities law problems, so sequence the asks to match the proof.

In plain English

A gate is a decision point. Before it, you spend a limited amount to reduce a specific risk. At the gate, you check whether the risk has fallen enough to justify the next, larger amount. If not, you stop or change course while the loss is still small.

Sequencing is the order in which risks are removed and money is raised. Early money is expensive because risk is high. Later money is cheaper because risk is lower. Good sequencing raises the smallest amount possible at the riskiest stage.

A condition precedent, covered in lesson 7, is something that must happen before a party is bound to perform. Lenders and investors write gates into their documents as conditions precedent.

The framework

A common sequence for a development, with the question each gate answers:

  1. Gate 1, site control. Is there an option or a conditional purchase agreement, with enough time for due diligence? Due diligence is the investigation of a property's legal, physical and financial facts.
  2. Gate 2, feasibility. Do title, zoning, environmental reports, servicing and a preliminary cost estimate support the plan?
  3. Gate 3, entitlement. Are the zoning approvals and development permits granted, or is the path to them clear and costed?
  4. Gate 4, cost certainty. Is there a detailed estimate or a fixed-price or guaranteed maximum price contract?
  5. Gate 5, financing. Are equity commitments signed and the construction loan term sheet accepted, with sources equal to uses?
  6. Gate 6, closing and draw. Are all conditions precedent in the loan satisfied so the first draw can be made?

Each gate should have a written checklist, a budget for reaching it, and a person who decides whether it has been passed.

Two rules make gates work. First, the spending before a gate should be small compared with what the gate protects. Second, the decision at the gate must be honest. A gate that is always passed, whatever the evidence says, is not a gate. Write down in advance what result would make you stop, so the decision is made against a standard and not against hope.

A legal point about raising equity. Selling shares or units in a project to investors is generally a distribution of securities, which in Canada requires a prospectus unless an exemption applies. National Instrument 45-106 Prospectus Exemptions sets out common exemptions, such as for accredited investors, and some require filings and offering documents. The details and the Alberta requirements must be confirmed with securities counsel. [unverified — confirm independently]

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A developer finds a site and wants to raise a hypothetical $3,000,000 of equity immediately.

Instead he sequences. He spends $50,000 for a 120-day purchase option. He spends $150,000 on feasibility: title search, environmental site assessment, geotechnical report and a cost consultant's estimate. The environmental report finds a small contamination issue with a hypothetical $200,000 cleanup cost, which he adds to the pro forma and uses to negotiate a $250,000 price reduction.

At Gate 2 he now has documented answers to the questions every investor will ask. He raises $400,000 of early-stage equity from a few accredited investors, under an exemption confirmed by counsel, to fund entitlement. Only after permits are granted and a fixed-price contract is negotiated does he raise the remaining equity, now at better terms because the risk is lower and the evidence is on the table.

Professional Sign-Off Required: securities lawyer, real estate lawyer, and chartered professional accountant

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is asking for all the money at the start, when risk is highest, so investors either refuse or demand a large share of the project. The second mistake is collecting money informally from friends and family without checking securities law. An unlawful distribution can give investors a right to their money back and expose the developer to penalties.

How you will use it

As a developer, write a gate plan for each project before you spend the first large dollar. List the gates, what must be true at each, what it costs to get there, and who decides. Match each fundraising ask to the gate it follows, and bring the gate evidence with you: the reports, the approvals, the contract, the term sheet. Talk to securities counsel before you take money from anyone outside your own companies. At each gate, be willing to stop. The money you do not spend on a project that fails a gate is money you keep for the one that passes.
checklist: Write the list of gates for the project before spending the first large dollar
Set what must be true, the budget and the decision-maker for each gate
Secure site control with enough due diligence time
Match each fundraising ask to the gate it follows
Bring the gate evidence to every lender or investor meeting
Speak to securities counsel before taking money from any outside investor
Decide in advance what result at each gate would make you stop

selftest.q: You have a signed purchase agreement but no environmental report, no zoning approval and no cost estimate. A friend offers to invest a large sum now. What should you consider?
selftest.a: You are before the feasibility gate, so risk is high and the terms will reflect it. It is usually better to spend a small amount to pass feasibility first, then raise larger amounts. Before taking any outside investor's money, confirm with securities counsel which prospectus exemption applies and what documents and filings are needed.

apply: For one project, write down the next gate, what must be true to pass it, what it will cost to get there, and who will decide.
sources: National Instrument 45-106 Prospectus Exemptions (Canadian Securities Administrators), details and Alberta requirements tagged unverified; confirm with the Alberta Securities Commission and securities counsel. Gate and sequencing practice is standard development management, not statute. All figures are hypothetical. Education only, not legal or financial advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: securities lawyer, real estate lawyer, and chartered professional accountant
